blocks.text: So far we have reviewed many names of locusts, scattered here and there in the Prophetic books. Lest anyone think they are wholly synonymous, it should be known that most of them denote definite species. This is clear from Ioel. I, 4., where what the gazam left the arbe ate, and what the arbe left the jelek ate, and what the jelek left the chasil ate. So it appears that gazam, arbe, jelek and chasil are distinct species ^{(13)}. Again, in Levit. XI, 21. 22. four species of locusts are counted, namely arbe, solam, chargol and chagab; common to all of these is that they are winged, four-footed, and permitted as food ^{(14)}. For the Arabs teach that locusts are [III, 260] distinguished in various ways. Damir: وهى اصناف فبعضه اصفر وبعضه ابيض وبعضه احمر وبعضه اسود وبعضه كبير الجثة وبعضه صغيرها [wa-hiya aṣnāf fa-baʿḍuhu aṣfar wa-baʿḍuhu abyaḍ wa-baʿḍuhu aḥmar wa-baʿḍuhu aswad wa-baʿḍuhu kabīr al-juththa wa-baʿḍuhu ṣaghīruhā] There are various species of locusts. For some are yellow, some white, some red, some black. Some are of large body, and some of small. But Marcellus Virgilius on Dioscorides, book 2, puts it much more eloquently: Nature has varied locusts with wonderful artistry, etc. For there are some that are green, some black, some livid, some that display this colour in one part and that in another. There are some that only when flying reveal a colour previously hidden. There are some that fly with single wings, some with several, some that lack wings and leap, some that, deprived of both these motions, only walk. There are some with longer legs, some with shorter: and among these, some with more and shorter joints, some with fewer and longer. There are some that sing, some that are mute, some that are heard by day, some only in the dark. And, not to be too long, there are some that do no harm to man in farming and harmlessly let themselves be caught by boys. There are others, on the contrary, that bring pestilence and ruin to all crops throughout whole regions, and by the famine they cause have often forced peoples to abandon their ancestral fields [col. 447]. Therefore, as there are different species of locusts, so there are also different names. Thus by reason of form or colour in Arabic سرعوف [surʿūf] surouph is the long locust, جندخ [jundukh] giondoch the fat locust, برقان [burqān] borkan the variegated locust, جردم [jardam] giardam the green locust with a black head ^{(15)}; conversely, كدم [kudam] chudam the black locust with a green head ^{(16)}. They are also distinguished by reason of place: حبشان [ḥubshān] chobsan is the Ethiopian locust; عرفان [ʿurfān] orphan, the one found in the sands of Aligi or Dahnae, [III, 261] near Medina; and by reason of sex, for the male locust is called عصغور [ʿuṣghūr] usphour ^{(17)}, and عظاري [ʿaẓārī] adari, and عسقول [ʿusqūl] uscoul; the female دباسا [dibāsā] dibasa, and عيسا [ʿaysā] aisa; and by reason of age, as these words of Damir prove: اذا خرج الجرد من بيضة يقال لها الدبا ^{(18)} فاذا طلعت اجنحته وكبرت فهو الغوغا وذلك حين عيوج بعضه في بعض فاذا بدت فيه الالوان واصفرت الذكور واسودت الاناث سمي جراد حينيذ [idhā kharaja al-jurd min bayḍa yuqāl lahā al-dabā fa-idhā ṭalaʿat ajniḥatuhu wa-kaburat fa-huwa al-ghawghā wa-dhālika ḥīna ʿywj baʿḍuhu fī baʿḍ fa-idhā badat fīhi al-alwān wa-iṣfarrat al-dhukūr wa-iswaddat al-ināth summiya jarād ḥīnaydh] When the locust comes out of the egg, it is called daba ^{(18)}; when the wings sprout and grow, it is called gauga, and that is when they swarm tumultuously over one another. But when they begin to be marked with various colours, so that the males turn yellow and the females black, then at last it is called girad ^{(19)}.

In Latin دبا [dabā] daba is the bruchus, غوغا [ghawghā] gauga the attelabus, and جراد [jarād] girad the locust, if these words of Remigius of Auxerre on Joel are true: The offspring or young of the locust, before it has wings, is called bruchus. Then, when it has begun to fly a little, it is called attelabus. Then, when it has begun to fly fully, it becomes a locust. And Jerome on Nahum III says much the same: That the bruchus does nothing else but stays always on the ground and, without wings, serves food and belly. The attelabus, however, takes on at least modest wings, and though it cannot fly high, it is nevertheless noted to leap up from the ground, and finally, becoming a locust, it flies, etc. And again: The attelabus, [III, 262] which Aquila more expressively rendered 'devourer', is a small locust between the locust and the bruchus, creeping rather than flying on small wings, and always leaping. For Augustine too, on Psalm 104, the bruchus is the offspring of the locust. The plague, he says, of the locust and of the bruchus is one; since the one is the parent and the other the offspring. And Isidore asserts that almost the whole body of the bruchus is gathered into the belly: that is, it is scarcely anything but belly, since it wholly lacks wings. He has this from Gregory on Job, book 33, ch. 17. Accordingly βροῦχος [brouchos], or βροῦκος [broukos], as the Ionians wrote it according to Hesychius, is so called παρὰ τὸ βρύκειν, τὸ ἐσθίειν [para to brykein, to esthiein], from eating or devouring, as μάσταξ [mastax] παρὰ τὸ μασᾶσθαι [para to masasthai], from chewing; as if it served nothing but the belly, being incapable of flight.
